extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of political science, journalism, civic educators, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Theory and practical guidance for understanding how public opinion is formed, how it misrepresents the real environment, and what journalists, teachers, and policymakers should do to bring public opinion into better contact with reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo-environment as determinant of behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the 'pseudo-environment' — the interior pictures or representations of the world that people construct and on which their behavior is a response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann: "It is the insertion between man and his environment of a pseudo-environment. To that pseudo-environment his behavior is a response." Consequence: actions motivated by the pseudo-environment operate in the real environment and can cause maladjustment; examples include misunderstandings in war, rumors, and individual superstitions (the girl who thought a cracked pane signalled a death). Analytic work must therefore uncover the pictures people hold, not assume direct access to reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maps/models must approximate the real environment
rubrics_metrics.description: People must use simplified 'maps' or models of the world to act, but these maps must be sufficiently accurate for the intended purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann argues that 'to traverse the world men must have maps of the world' and warns that 'their persistent difficulty is to secure maps on which their own need ... has not sketched in the coast of Bohemia.' Examples: flat‑earth belief, Ponce de Leon seeking a fountain because of an imagined map, digging up yellow dirt mistaken for gold. When models diverge from facts, actions based on them produce maladjustment ('butting one's head against a stone wall').

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish fiction (models) from deliberate falsehoods
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat 'fictions' as representations of the environment with varying degrees of fidelity, not simply as lies; recognize their legitimate role as schematic models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann: 'By fictions I do not mean lies. I mean a representation of the environment which is in lesser or greater degree made by man himself.' Guidance: accept schematic models and approximations (including scientists' models) so long as their degree of fidelity is taken into account; beware of conflating useful simplification with deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbols and personified images govern public behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion is often organized around symbolic personalities and images rather than detailed facts; these symbols shape emotion and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: hero-worship of generals (Joffre), the constructed public persona of monarchs, the quick personification of enemies (the Kaiser) or saviors. Symbols can unite whole populations briefly (war) or be more fragmented in normal times; analysts must examine the scope and inclusiveness of such symbols and how they coalesce, fray, or shift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspect and evaluate information sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach and practice rigorous source evaluation: check where a dispatch was filed, the correspondent's name, the press service, the authority cited, and whether the reporter saw what he describes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann recommends that teachers 'teach the pupil to look in his newspaper for the place where the dispatch was filed, for the name of the correspondent, the name of the press service, the authority given for the statement, the circumstances under which the statement was secured.' Use the case method to train habits of source scrutiny; this is essential to prevent acting on rumors or partisan fabrications (Senate marines example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligence work / reporting must supply a valid picture of the environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Political criticism, teaching, and decision-making depend on expert reporters and intelligence work that provide usable, valid pictures of the relevant environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann: 'Unless he can count upon receiving from expert reporters a valid picture of the environment, his dialectic cannot go far.' The collection of social data should become a routine accompaniment to action; accurate reporting reduces maladjustment and improves the capacity of political science and civic education to guide behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic education: teach study of error and scientific habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Civic education should cultivate awareness of mental subjectivism, teach the history of stereotypes and propaganda, and use the study of error as a path to objective method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use history, comparative anthropology, and case studies to 'produce a life-long realization of the way codes impose a special pattern upon the imagination.' Lippmann argues the study of error is 'in the highest degree prophylactic' and can stimulate appreciation for scientific method; teachers should show how allegory, dramatization, and personification shape opinion and encourage introspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for the time-differential between reason and action
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the practicability of plans and critique by considering the time required for reason, data-collection, and implementation versus the urgency of political action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann stresses that 'the rate at which reason ... can advance itself is slower than the rate at which action has to be taken.' Analysts should distinguish false crises from real ones, calculate whether the data a plan assumes will still hold by the time it is executed, and factor time into political strategy and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspend emotional judgment until facts are verified
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid letting need or partisanship convert rumors into assumed facts; cultivate procedures to delay policy responses until investigation yields reliable information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the Senate episode where Senators assumed a partisan-friendly report about marines without verifying it. Even trained professionals can succumb to credulity when a fiction is 'badly needed.' Institutional habits (resolutions to investigate, forensic inquiry) and source-checking are the remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and analyze propaganda as an active shaper of pictures
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda is the deliberate effort to alter the pictures to which people respond; understanding propaganda is central to understanding political behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann: 'What is propaganda, if not the effort to alter the picture to which men respond?' Analysts and teachers must study past propaganda, censorship, and privacy practices to reveal how public images are manufactured and how they can be countered or corrected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simplification strategically but account for its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Schematic models and stylized representations are necessary because the real environment is too complex, but their limits and the purposes for which they are adequate must be explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann notes the alternative to fiction would be direct exposure to raw sensation, which is infeasible; thus simplifications are indispensable. However, one must 'take into account' the degree of fidelity and avoid letting simplification become habitual blindness to relevant facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral norms in appeals to reason: reject hatred, secrecy, lying
rubrics_metrics.description: When making an appeal to reason in public life, exclude hatred, intolerance, suspicion, bigotry, secrecy, fear, and lying — they are poisons to public reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann lists these seven as 'the seven deadly sins against public opinion' and argues that taking a long view and cultivating decency are necessary for reason to function in politics; though not always provable, decency is necessary for constructive discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education as long-term remedy depends on evolving social knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The efficacy of education in aligning public opinion with reality depends on the accumulation and evolution of reliable social knowledge and routine information-gathering linked to action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann: 'The value of this education will depend upon the evolution of knowledge. And our knowledge of human institutions is still extraordinarily meager and impressionistic.' Therefore institutionalize social data collection and make it a normal part of decision-making so civic education has substantive material to teach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine the scope and limits of symbolic pictures in times of security vs crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand that symbolic pictures are broader, more unifying, and more emotionally charged in crises (e.g., wartime hero-worship) and narrower, contested, and checked by argument in normal times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann contrasts wartime wholesale symbolization (unity around a hero) with peacetime pluralism where symbols 'come and go, coalesce and are forgotten.' Analysts should therefore treat symbols differently depending on social context and expect rapid change after crises (e.g., Allied Unity collapsing after armistice).
